This project classifies particle types (electrons, positrons, muons, pions, and protons) from liquid argon time projection chamber detector images using convolutional neural networks. Building on the MicroBooNE Collaboration’s approach [1], the model learns visual patterns directly from the data rather than relying on hand-engineered physics rules. Through systematic hyperparameter optimization focused on learning rate scheduling, the final model achieves 89.1% validation accuracy.
Source code: github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/high-energy-particle-classifier

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
text:

This dataset contains five charged particle types commonly observed in liquid argon time projection chambers. Each particle differs in mass and electric charge, which strongly influences its track morphology in the detector.

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
section: Example Particle Tracks Across the Momentum Range
text:
Example Particle Tracks Across the Momentum Range
The figure below shows example detector images for each particle type, ordered by increasing initial momentum from left to right. Each row shows one of three detector projections (X–Y, Y–Z, Z–X).
Higher-mass particles produce shorter, denser tracks, while lighter particles travel farther and scatter more. These subtle visual differences are what the CNN learns to distinguish.

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
text:
Truth-Level Feature Distributions
Each detector image comes with kinematic and spatial features that provide physical context for the particle trajectories.
The momentum components \(p_x\), \(p_y\), and \(p_z\) are symmetric around zero since particles are equally likely to move in any direction. Total momentum is defined as \(p = \sqrt{p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2}\).
The production coordinates \((x, y, z)\) are bounded and approximately uniform, reflecting the detector geometry.

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
text:
Architecture
The model uses a convolutional neural network with three conv blocks, each containing two convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU activation. After each block, max pooling reduces spatial dimensions while dropout provides regularization. The feature maps start at 16 filters and double with each block (16 → 32 → 64), allowing the network to learn increasingly abstract representations of particle tracks.
Global average pooling compresses the final feature maps into a fixed-length vector, which feeds into a small dense layer before the 5-way softmax classifier. This architecture balances expressiveness with efficiency. It is simple enough to train quickly, but with enough capacity to capture the visual patterns that distinguish particle types.

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
text:
Initial Model Performance

Training Dynamics
The model learns quickly, with training and validation accuracy tracking closely. The final training accuracy is 82.9% and validation accuracy is 82.4%, suggesting minimal overfitting.











Classification Performance
Electrons, positrons, and protons are classified with high accuracy, while muons and pions show more confusion with other particle types. This may be due to particle tracks with similar energies looking visually alike.

title: High Energy Particle CNN Classifier
text:
Performance Evaluation

Training Dynamics
The final model trained for 14 epochs with learning rate plateau scheduling. Training was stable throughout, with the learning rate reducing from 1e-3 to 2e-4 at epoch 9, and again to 4e-5 at epoch 12 as validation loss plateaued. The model achieved peak validation accuracy of 89.1% at epoch 10, with training and validation curves remaining close, indicating good generalization without overfitting.











Classification Performance
The final model achieves 89.1% validation accuracy - a 6.7 percentage point improvement over the baseline. The confusion matrix shows much better distinction between muons and pions, which were the most challenging classes initially.





Example predictions show the model correctly classifying particles across different momentum ranges and track morphologies.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
The 85% Problem
Most machine learning projects fail. Not because the algorithms don’t work, but because organizations can’t operationalize them. A 2024 analysis found that 85% of ML initiatives never deliver business value in production (Galileo), a staggering figure for technology that many companies are betting their futures and resources on.
The pattern is familiar to anyone who’s worked in data science. A team spends months developing a model. The metrics look perfect, the stakeholders are excited, and six months from now everyone will have quietly moved on, the model still trapped in a Jupyter notebook. The graveyard of promising models is vast.
This isn’t a talent problem or a tools problem. It’s an infrastructure problem. The discipline that addresses it, MLOps, has become the difference between organizations that extract value from ML and those that don’t.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
The Problem

Somewhere in your organization, a data scientist is building a model that will never see the light of day. The metrics look perfect, the stakeholders are excited, and six months from now everyone will have quietly moved on, the model still trapped in a Jupyter notebook. This is not a failure of machine learning. It is a failure of infrastructure, of process, and the complexities between “it works on my laptop” and “it works at scale, reliably, for millions of users.”
Consider what happens when models do make it to production. An e-commerce company spends months developing a recommendation system that achieves strong performance on test sets and shows promising results in A/B testing, but when deployed, the model’s performance degrades significantly within weeks. The training data might have been collected during a holiday season, causing the model to learn patterns specific to that period that don’t generalize to normal shopping behavior. Without proper monitoring and drift detection, this degradation goes unnoticed until customer complaints about irrelevant recommendations start piling up. This scenario, documented in case studies from companies like Zalando and Netflix, illustrates how operational constraints often cause more production failures than algorithmic problems themselves (Zalando case study, Netflix RecSysOps).
When models do see the light of day, they often fail in ways that take months to notice. An e-commerce company I spoke with spent the better part of a year developing a recommendation system. Test performance was strong. A/B results looked promising. Within weeks of deployment, the whole thing started falling apart. The culprit was banal: the training data had been collected during a holiday season, and the model had learned shopping patterns that evaporated once normal life resumed. Without drift detection, nobody noticed until customer complaints about bizarre recommendations reached a critical mass. Case studies from Zalando and Netflix tell similar stories. Operational failures, it turns out, cause more production problems than algorithmic ones (Zalando case study, Netflix RecSysOps).

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
What Makes ML Different

You could describe MLOps as DevOps for machine learning, but that undersells the strangeness of what we’re dealing with. Traditional software is, in a sense, honest. You write code, you test it, you deploy it, and it does what you told it to do. Machine learning systems are different. They are shaped by data in ways that make them unpredictable, even to the people who built them.
The same code can produce wildly different outputs as data distributions shift. A model that worked brilliantly yesterday might fail tomorrow, and nothing in the codebase will have changed. Performance degrades as the real world drifts away from the world captured in training data. Random seeds, hardware quirks, and dependency versions conspire to make reproducibility a constant struggle. And in regulated industries, you need explainability and audit trails that traditional software never demanded.
The seminal paper on this subject, “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems,” put it starkly: the ML code itself represents only a tiny fraction of a production system’s complexity. The rest is data collection, feature extraction, configuration, serving infrastructure, and monitoring. The model is the easy part (Sculley et al., 2015).
Uber learned this the hard way with their ETA predictions. Models trained on San Francisco traffic failed catastrophically in Mumbai. Models that worked in January degraded by March as patterns shifted. Their solution was to build automated pipelines that monitor accuracy and trigger retraining without human intervention, a system that required feature stores, model registries, and testing infrastructure that rivals anything in traditional software engineering (Uber Michelangelo, DeepETA).

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
Why It Matters Now

For years, machine learning lived in the back office. It powered internal analytics, batch processing, things that happened overnight while everyone slept. That era is over. ChatGPT handles hundreds of millions of conversations every week. Voice assistants respond in real time. Recommendation algorithms shape what billions of people see, read, and buy. Search engines have started generating answers instead of just pointing to them.
When machine learning moves from analytics to product, everything changes. A notebook model can take hours to run. A consumer product must respond in milliseconds. A notebook model can fail quietly. A consumer product that fails visibly destroys trust. A notebook model can be retrained whenever someone gets around to it. A consumer product must adapt continuously without going dark.
Netflix processes billions of interactions daily while simultaneously retraining the models that power recommendations. This requires coordinating hundreds of models across multiple services, a feat of orchestration that would have seemed absurd a decade ago (Netflix Maestro, Netflix foundation model).
Large language models have made all of this more urgent. They power chatbots and coding assistants and creative tools, but they also introduce failure modes we’re only beginning to understand: hallucinations, prompt injection attacks, outputs that seem confident but are completely wrong. LLMOps, as practitioners have started calling it, focuses less on training from scratch and more on prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and figuring out how to deploy responsibly (OpenAI Realtime API).
Regulators have noticed. The EU AI Act now requires organizations to demonstrate model governance, explainability, and auditability. Research suggests that 85% of ML projects fail to deliver business value in production, often because of silent failures, distribution drift, and pipeline breaks that nobody catches until real damage is done (ML Observability Framework). In consumer-facing applications, these failures aren’t silent at all. Users notice. Revenue suffers.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
What You Actually Need

A startup with one model has different needs than a bank running hundreds of risk models. Still, certain components show up everywhere.
Version control needs to extend beyond code. Models, data, configurations, and experiments all need versioning because the relationships between them determine how models behave. Tools like DVC, MLflow, and Weights & Biases can track the full lineage from raw data to deployment. This becomes critical when you need to understand, months later, why a model made a particular decision.
Reproducible environments matter more than people expect. A model trained with TensorFlow 2.8 might produce different outputs when deployed with TensorFlow 2.9, even with identical weights. Changes in numerical precision and optimization algorithms can shift results in subtle ways. Strict containerization and pinned dependencies are the only reliable defense.
Testing has to happen at multiple levels because ML systems fail in ways traditional software doesn’t. You need unit tests for data processing, integration tests for pipelines, validation tests for data quality and schema drift, performance tests against accuracy thresholds, and infrastructure tests for deployment configurations.
Monitoring splits into three domains. System monitoring tracks the usual suspects: CPU, memory, latency. Data monitoring watches feature distributions, missing values, schema changes. Model monitoring tracks prediction distributions, accuracy over time, and drift. Tools like Evidently AI and WhyLabs can help, though custom dashboards on Prometheus and Grafana remain common.

Airbnb discovered something subtle about their pricing models: individual predictions looked reasonable, but in aggregate, the system was pricing every property in certain neighborhoods too high during peak periods. Catching this required monitoring not just individual outputs but aggregate patterns and business metrics (Airbnb pricing).
A model registry centralizes metadata, performance metrics, and approval workflows, making it possible to roll back when something goes wrong. Feature stores solve the problem of teams reimplementing the same feature engineering logic across projects, introducing inconsistencies that are maddening to debug. Uber’s Palette system serves features for both real-time inference and training, ensuring that what the model learned matches what it sees in production (Uber Palette).

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
The Hard Part

None of this is primarily a technology problem. The hardest part is organizational.
Data scientists, ML engineers, DevOps engineers, and product managers need to work together in ways that traditional corporate structures actively discourage. Silos that took years to build have to come down. The culture has to shift from “move fast and break things” toward something more like “move deliberately and watch everything.”
MLOps demands a blend of data science, software engineering, and infrastructure expertise that few individuals possess. Some organizations have responded by creating dedicated ML platform teams that build tooling and infrastructure, freeing data scientists to focus on modeling while platform engineers handle operational complexity.
Perhaps the deepest challenge is defining what success actually means. Traditional software metrics like uptime and latency don’t capture what matters for ML systems. A recommendation engine might boost click-through rates while trapping users in filter bubbles. A fraud detection system might achieve high accuracy while flagging so many legitimate transactions that customers abandon ship. These tradeoffs require judgment that spans both technical and business domains, and organizations that can’t make those judgments well tend to build systems that optimize for the wrong things.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
Getting Started

If you’re starting from scratch, resist the urge to build everything at once. Version your models and data first. Even basic versioning provides enormous value and creates the foundation for everything else. Add monitoring next, starting simple: prediction distributions, latency, error rates. Pick one manual process and automate it, whether that’s deployment or retraining or testing. Learn from that before expanding.
The organizations that succeed tend to start with their biggest pain points rather than with some idealized architecture. MLOps is iterative. You build what you need, discover new problems, and build again.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
Why This Matters

MLOps is no longer optional. As machine learning moves from research curiosity to production infrastructure, organizations that invest in operational excellence will pull ahead. More importantly, robust operations are becoming a prerequisite for responsible deployment.
The models we build now influence loan approvals, medical diagnoses, hiring decisions, and resource allocation at a scale that would have been unimaginable a decade ago. Deploying these systems without proper monitoring, governance, and operational discipline isn’t just bad engineering. It is, in a meaningful sense, reckless.
The future of this field isn’t just about building better models. It’s about building models that work reliably, transparently, and ethically once they leave the notebook. MLOps is the bridge that makes that possible.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
section: The Failure Rate Nobody Talks About
text:
The Failure Rate Nobody Talks About
A recent analysis found that 85% of machine learning projects never deliver business value in production (Galileo). That number should be shocking, but if you’ve spent time in the industry, it probably isn’t. You’ve seen the pattern: a team spends months on a model, the accuracy metrics look strong, leadership gets excited, and then the project stalls somewhere between “working prototype” and “deployed system.” Or it launches, degrades quietly, and gets shut down a year later when someone finally audits it.
The problem isn’t that machine learning doesn’t work. The problem is that most organizations have no idea how to run it in production. They’ve hired data scientists, bought cloud compute, maybe even acquired some promising startups. What they haven’t done is build the operational infrastructure that turns experimental models into reliable systems. The industry has started calling this infrastructure MLOps, a name that doesn’t do justice to how important it is.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
Where Things Go Wrong
The most common failure isn’t a bad algorithm. It’s a good model that slowly stops working because nobody’s watching it.
Machine learning models are trained on historical data, but the world doesn’t stay still. Customer preferences shift. Competitors change their pricing. Fraud patterns evolve. A recommendation model trained on last year’s behavior might be confidently suggesting products that nobody wants anymore. Zalando documented this happening to their own systems; accuracy degraded substantially before anyone noticed, and by then the user experience damage was done (Zalando).
The second class of failures is more subtle. During training, a model learns from features computed by one pipeline. In production, those same features get computed by a different system, often built by a different team. Small inconsistencies creep in. A timestamp gets parsed differently. A null value gets handled differently. The model sees data that doesn’t quite match what it learned from, and its predictions suffer. Uber built their entire Michelangelo platform largely to eliminate this problem, which tells you how serious it is (Uber).
Then there’s the reproducibility problem, which tends to bite at the worst times. Someone needs to retrain a model that’s been running for a year. The original data scientist has left. The notebook they used references data that’s been moved, dependencies that have been updated, and parameters that were tweaked by hand and never recorded. Reconstructing the model becomes archaeology. I’ve watched teams spend weeks trying to reproduce results that took days to generate originally.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
What Operational Maturity Looks Like
The organizations that consistently get value from ML have built infrastructure that most companies lack.
They version everything, not just code. Training data, model weights, feature definitions, hyperparameters, environment configurations. The goal is to answer a simple question: what exactly produced this prediction? If you can’t reconstruct a model’s lineage on demand, you can’t audit decisions, debug production issues, or reliably retrain. Tools like DVC and MLflow help, but plenty of organizations still haven’t adopted them systematically (DVC, MLflow).
They’ve centralized feature management. Once you’re running more than a handful of models, having each team compute its own features becomes a liability. Definitions diverge. Training and serving get out of sync. Bugs become nearly impossible to trace. Feature stores provide a single source of truth, and the good ones serve features with low enough latency for real-time inference while maintaining exact parity with offline training. Uber’s Palette handles millions of lookups per second this way (Palette).
They monitor at multiple levels. Traditional application monitoring, the kind that tracks latency and error rates, isn’t enough. You also need to track the distribution of predictions, the drift in input features, and actual model accuracy when ground truth becomes available. Airbnb learned this when they discovered their pricing models were systematically overpricing certain neighborhoods. Individual predictions looked reasonable; only business-level monitoring revealed the aggregate problem (Airbnb).

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
section: The Part That Isn’t About Technology
text:
The Part That Isn’t About Technology
The tools exist. The harder problem is organizational.
Data scientists and engineers have different objectives. Data scientists want to maximize model performance. Engineers want systems that are reliable, maintainable, and don’t page them at 3am. These goals aren’t always compatible, and without deliberate effort to align them, the handoff from research to production becomes adversarial. I’ve seen promising models die in that gap because neither side felt ownership of getting them across.
Some companies have addressed this by creating dedicated platform teams that build ML infrastructure for everyone else. Others have invested in a hybrid role, the ML engineer, who can work on both sides of the divide. What doesn’t work is treating production deployment as someone else’s problem.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
section: Large Language Models Have Made This Urgent
text:
Large Language Models Have Made This Urgent
LLMs compress timelines and raise stakes. Organizations expect to deploy AI capabilities in weeks now, not quarters. The models power customer-facing products with failure modes we’re still learning to handle: hallucinations, prompt injection, outputs that sound authoritative but are wrong. They require specialized infrastructure for inference at scale.
The operational challenges differ from traditional ML. There’s less focus on training and more on prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and figuring out how to evaluate outputs that don’t have clean right-or-wrong answers. But the core lesson is the same: the gap between “working demo” and “production system” is where most initiatives fail.

title: Why Your ML Models Aren’t Making It to Production
text:
The Compounding Advantage
The 85% failure rate isn’t distributed evenly. Organizations with mature operations deploy models faster, catch problems earlier, and build institutional knowledge that compounds. Those without keep investing in data science while watching projects stall.
The gap will widen. As ML becomes infrastructure rather than experiment, the ability to operate it reliably becomes the bottleneck. Companies that solve MLOps will be able to use AI. Everyone else will keep running pilots.

title: January 2026
text:
What I Created

This Website
This month I made this website with Quarto. It went through a few iterations before I landed on a relatively minimal design. My first paid job (I was 13, and it was probably not compliant with child labor laws) was building a website for a restaurant on the high street in my hometown. This one turned out much better. Web design has become a lot easier since then.


Particle Classifier Project
I revisited and updated one of my earlier CNN projects, exploring additional hyperparameter optimisation and running new experiments. It was interesting to come back to this work while taking a graduate machine learning course, which has been deepening my understanding of my previous projects.


Private Social Media Project
I’ve been exploring web app design by building a social media app for private use. It’s been useful to think more deliberately about user experience and user journeys, rather than focusing purely on technical or data-driven perspectives.


Vegetables
I had a huge harvest of tomatoes, basil, and aubergines from my hydroponic tower this month. I made this caponata recipe from Nourishing Amy, and it turned out great!

title: January 2026
text:
What I Learned

Mandarin
My husband and I have been learning Mandarin as our New Year’s resolution. When we were in high school, he became fluent in Japanese in a few months because he wanted to read Japanese murder mysteries. I’ve studied Mandarin a few times before, at the University of Hong Kong and through the Confucius Institute, but I have significant difficulty processing spoken language. When it comes to learning languages, my mind can feel like a sieve, and I lose skills quickly if I don’t use them regularly.
This time, I want to approach it differently by integrating Mandarin into my daily routine through flashcards and writing practice. We’re also doing a weekly session using a textbook from one of my previous courses. It has been fun to revisit, and I’ve found that I’m remembering characters more quickly than I expected.


207 ML Concepts
This semester in the MIDS program, I’m taking Machine Learning. It’s still early, but I’m enjoying the examples we’ve been introduced to so far, as well as the chance to have my skills tested through different projects. It’s been helpful to revisit familiar ideas in a more formal framework while also being pushed into new ways of thinking about them.

title: January 2026
text:
What I Reflected on

Album

Oil of Every Pearl’s Un-Insides - SOPHIE
When I got a record player a few years ago, this was one of the first albums I bought, and I still come back to it often. The whole album feels ahead of its time, but it still balances a certain ancient, human quality. Lately I’ve been listening a lot to “Is It Cold in the Water?”, and depending on where and how I hear it, it becomes a completely different experience. On vinyl it sounds eerie, sad, and lonely, like an old god being forced to adapt to the times. But when I’m walking somewhere with headphones, it transforms into a story about seeking growth and taking the plunge, pushing through apprehension, and moving past the inertia that stems from fearing change.
This month especially, I’ve enjoyed returning to it because it keeps circling themes of consciousness and the relationship between the physical body, the mind, and the spirit, which are themes I’ve been exploring through other media and writing. A new year brings new challenges and unfamiliar territory, and this album understands both the pain and the euphoria of becoming someone new.




Article

An Act of Cosmic Sabotage - Ross Andersen
I was disappointed to learn that the Mars Sample Return mission associated with Perseverance is being defunded. Sample return has long been understood as the necessary next step in Mars exploration and astrobiology. Without it, much of the scientific value of in situ rover work remains unresolved, and years of planning, engineering, and data collection risk being left incomplete.
Both my bachelor’s and master’s theses focused on applying machine learning and statistical methods to Mars exploration. My undergraduate work, in particular, centred on diagnosing hydration states of magnesium salts using Raman spectroscopy, which is the same technique Perseverance uses for in situ analysis. Sample return would allow much higher resolution laboratory analysis, which would be incredibly informative for future missions and work.
The current administration’s continued defunding of scientific programmes at NASA will likely have effects that extend well beyond a single mission. Fields that depend on long-term continuity, like astrobiology, are especially vulnerable, and the consequences of these decisions will be felt for decades rather than years.




Artwork

Te Quiero Inti - Miguel Arzabe
I saw this piece during my recent visit to the de Young Museum and I was drawn to the texture the artist creates by weaving strips of canvas together. The technique is inspired by Bolivian weaving, and it gives the work a very tactile, lively feel. I also love that it’s so personal: the piece celebrates the artist’s daughter, who’s named after Inti, the Quechua sun god.




Book

Data Detective - Tim Harford
For my Research Design class last semester, we read Data Detective. I learned a lot from it, including that Florence Nightingale created polar diagrams. I honoured her in my own work by making my first visualization a polar diagram.
As someone with a physics background, my training has predisposed me to put a lot of weight on data and numerical outcomes. Physics experiments are often fairly clean-cut, and relationships are usually well enough understood to directly connect theory and evidence. This book was a good reminder to approach statistics and data with skepticism, especially when definitions are not precise, as is often the case with surveys and other forms of human data collection.




Manga

Uzumaki - Junji Ito
I visited the Manga exhibition at the de Young this month, and it inspired me to return to reading Junji Ito’s Uzumaki. Uzumaki is a horror manga about spirals. You may think, spirals? What’s scary about spirals? But let me assure you, Junji Ito can do some pretty twisted things with the motif of spirals. He manages to translate a sense of doom and rising tension about something that shouldn’t be horrifying. Plus the art is just so cool.




Film

Ran - Akira Kurosawa
I have been obsessed with Akira Kurosawa since I saw Dreams last year at The Roxie Theatre. I then watched Ran with my parents when they visited last March, and later ended up buying a ticket to the Akira Kurosawa four-movie event in September.
They didn’t like the movie much. It was subtitled, and they didn’t bring their glasses. I loved it, and I wanted to watch it again this January because of how the film explores rebirth through the augmentation of power, and the tension between flattery and truth. It feels especially relevant in the current climate, where yes men are raised to the highest ranks of government.
Hidetora is an interesting character, because he is both a victim and perpertrator of violence. Until this point in time, he has been insulated from the pain he causes others, because of his station in life and physicality. But age strips him of this, and he is finally forced to confront his own hubris, especially when he encounters a victim of one of his expansionist campaigns, a man he blinded, and whose family he destroyed.
I also love a great battle scene, and this has one of the best I’ve seen. Red and yellow flags converge and the ground is so dark it barely feels like Earth anymore.




Memory

Cambodia 2020
When I think of new years and new beginnings, a strong memory I have is of watching the sunrise at 4am over Angkor Wat, stumbling over jagged edges in the dark, disoriented on three hours of sleep while solo travelling. I went to Siem Reap in January 2020 and stayed with Sophat, a tuk-tuk driver and Airbnb host who rented out one of the rooms in his family home to me. I ate some incredible fruit on that trip.
The whole experience has a haze to it in my memory, probably because that first day I was so sleep-deprived that everything felt slow and slightly unreal. I’ve always been attracted to places of religion, because they often hold the history and power of a community, and they’re monuments to art and divinity. Angkor Wat is huge and magical, and Mother Nature is always trying to reclaim and reintegrate it into the environment. Roots push the stones apart (tripping hazard, beware), and huge trees break through, or sometimes even support, the structures.





TV Show

Pluribus
Pluribus explores alternative forms of communication and the meaning of community through a really interesting lens. I find the idea of a hivemind compelling, and many of the issues the show raises feel very relevant to current AI adoption. Like an LLM, the hive operates with explicit guardrails meant to prevent violence or harm to living beings. At the same time, it finds ways to work around those constraints through emotional manipulation and underhanded strategies to gain control over characters who remain unjoined.
The parallels to sycophancy in AI are clear. As more people turn to AI systems for emotional support or decision-making, that tendency becomes increasingly troubling. With AI products becoming more monetised, for example through companies like OpenAI moving toward advertising models, I worry there will be less incentive to actively reduce sycophancy or strengthen existing protections.




Video Essay

Disney’s Living Characters: A Broken Promise - Defunctland
Disney has long positioned itself as an innovator, and this video essay traces decades of R&D around its idea of “Living Characters.” Yes, it is over four hours long. But it goes into incredibly detailed and thoughtful discussion of the logistical and technical challenges involved in creating live, responsive character experiences using robots and animatronics.
I enjoyed how the technology developed was framed primarily as an experience rather than as a tool. Designing systems meant to imitate life, be emotionally coherent, and safe for unpredictable human interaction requires a very different set of constraints than most technical projects. That perspective made me rethink how I approach design more generally, especially in contexts where users are not just interacting with a system, but forming expectations and emotional responses to it.
The essay also discusses an experimental AI fortune-teller robot called Destini, which used relatively simple computer vision to respond live to guests. Although it was never deployed in parks, it raises interesting questions about how AI could be incorporated into character-based experiences in the future.
Disney’s intense focus on protecting its IP makes this especially complex. Any character AI would need to be carefully constrained to avoid breaking immersion, violating brand expectations, or creating negative guest experiences. In that sense, the challenges Disney faced feel closely related to broader questions about deploying AI in emotionally charged, public-facing environments like healthcare.

This project implements an end-to-end receipt processing system that combines optical character recognition (OCR) with a multi-task neural network for sentence classification and named entity recognition (NER). The system scans receipt images, extracts text using OCR, and then processes the text with a BGE-M3 transformer backbone to classify sentences and extract entities. By leveraging pre-trained sentence embeddings and joint optimization, the model learns shared representations that benefit both tasks.
Source code: github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/sentence-project

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Receipt Image Processing
The system begins with receipt images captured via camera or uploaded as files. OCR technology extracts text from these images, handling challenges like:

Varied receipt formats: Different store layouts, fonts, and structures
Image quality: Blurry photos, poor lighting, or low resolution
Text orientation: Rotated or skewed text
Mixed content: Barcodes, logos, and text

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
OCR Implementation
The project uses Tesseract OCR (via pytesseract) for text extraction, with preprocessing steps to improve accuracy:

Image preprocessing: Grayscale conversion, noise reduction, contrast enhancement
Text detection: Automatic text region detection and orientation correction
Line segmentation: Splitting OCR output into individual lines and sentences

import pytesseract
from PIL import Image
import cv2

def preprocess_receipt_image(image_path):
    """Preprocess receipt image for better OCR accuracy"""
    img = cv2.imread(image_path)
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    # Apply denoising and thresholding
    denoised = cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising(gray)
    _, thresh = cv2.threshold(denoised, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
    return thresh

def extract_text_from_receipt(image_path):
    """Extract text from receipt image using OCR"""
    processed_img = preprocess_receipt_image(image_path)
    text = pytesseract.image_to_string(processed_img, config='--psm 6')
    return text

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Text Segmentation
After OCR extraction, the raw text is segmented into sentences using:

Rule-based segmentation: Period, newline, and punctuation-based splitting
Sentence boundary detection: Handling abbreviations and decimal numbers
Line grouping: Combining related lines that belong to the same logical sentence

The segmented sentences are then tokenized and prepared for the transformer model.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Model Choice: BGE-M3
The project uses the BGE-M3 (BAAI General Embedding) model by the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, selected for its strong performance across multiple NLP tasks. BGE-M3 is optimized for multi-task learning and provides:

Generalized embeddings: High-quality sentence representations that capture semantic meaning
Efficient architecture: Lightweight enough for practical applications while maintaining accuracy
Multi-task optimization: Pre-trained to support diverse NLP tasks simultaneously
Rich token-level representations: Essential for token-level tasks like NER

The model generates 1024-dimensional embeddings that encode semantic information in a dense vector space, enabling downstream tasks to leverage these rich representations.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Sentence Embeddings
Each sentence is encoded into a fixed-length vector where semantically similar sentences are positioned close together in the embedding space. The BGE-M3 model processes input text and produces normalized embeddings that capture:

Semantic meaning and context
Syntactic structure
Domain-specific patterns

For a batch of 15 example sentences, the model produces embeddings of shape [15, 1024], where each row represents one sentence’s encoding in the 1024-dimensional space.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Sentence Similarity
The embedding space enables similarity computation between sentences. Cosine similarity measures the angle between embedding vectors, with values close to 1 indicating high semantic similarity and values near 0 indicating dissimilarity.
This property is crucial for: - Semantic search: Finding documents or sentences similar to a query - Clustering: Grouping related sentences together - Classification: Using similarity as a feature for downstream tasks

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Clustering and Visualization
Using K-Means clustering on the embeddings reveals natural groupings of semantically similar sentences. When visualized with t-SNE dimensionality reduction, sentences cluster together based on shared themes, topics, or structures.
For receipt processing, this means sentences about products, prices, and store information naturally separate in the embedding space, making classification more effective.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Shared Transformer Backbone
The architecture builds on the pre-trained BGE-M3 transformer, which serves as a shared backbone for both tasks. The transformer processes input text and produces:

CLS token embedding: A global sentence representation from the special classification token
Token-level embeddings: Per-token representations for the entire sequence

These outputs are routed to two separate task-specific heads that learn specialized patterns for their respective tasks.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Sentence Classification Head
The classification head categorizes entire sentences into predefined classes (Product Name, Store Name, Price, Other). The architecture consists of:

First Linear Layer: Maps the 1024-dimensional CLS embedding to 128 dimensions, reducing dimensionality for efficiency
ReLU Activation: Introduces non-linearity to learn complex patterns while promoting sparse activations
Second Linear Layer: Maps to the final number of classes (4 categories)

The head uses only the CLS token representation, which is trained to capture global sentence meaning during pre-training.
self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(base_model.config.hidden_size, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, num_classes)
)

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Named Entity Recognition Head
The NER head performs token-level classification to identify entities within sentences. Unlike sentence classification, NER requires predictions for each token in the sequence.
The architecture is simpler—a single linear layer that maps each token’s hidden state to NER label logits:
self.ner_head = nn.Linear(base_model.config.hidden_size, num_ner_labels)
The model predicts one of five labels per token: - O: Outside entity (not part of any entity) - B-PRODUCT: Beginning of a product name - I-PRODUCT: Inside of a product name - B-PRICE: Beginning of a price entity - I-PRICE: Inside of a price entity
This BIO tagging scheme allows the model to identify multi-token entities like “500g Organic Canned Tomatoes” or “$32.66”.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Architecture Visualization
The diagram below illustrates how input text flows through the transformer backbone and is routed to both task-specific heads:

Input: Tokenized receipt sentences
Transformer: BGE-M3 processes tokens and produces hidden states
CLS Token: Extracted for sentence-level classification
All Tokens: Used for token-level NER predictions
Outputs: Classification logits and NER label logits

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Freezing Strategy
The project implements a freezing strategy that balances computational efficiency with task adaptation:

Freezing the Transformer Backbone
Advantages: - Only task-specific heads are updated, significantly reducing computational cost - Training is faster since the large transformer parameters remain fixed - Leverages high-quality pre-trained embeddings without modification
Trade-offs: - Limited adaptation if the target domain differs significantly from pre-training data - May not capture domain-specific nuances in the transformer layers
For receipt processing, freezing the backbone is effective because: - BGE-M3 embeddings are general enough to capture receipt text patterns - The task-specific heads can adapt to receipt-specific categories - Computational efficiency is important for practical deployment


Alternative Freezing Strategies
Freezing the entire network: Fastest but least flexible—useful for inference-only scenarios.
Freezing one task head: Useful when one task is well-learned but the other needs adaptation, though this risks imbalanced learning.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Transfer Learning

Pre-Trained Model Selection
BGE-M3 was chosen because it: - Supports multi-task learning natively - Provides both sentence-level and token-level representations - Is efficient and scalable for production use - Was trained on diverse text, making it suitable for receipt processing


Layer Freezing Rationale
In practice, the transformer backbone is frozen while task-specific heads remain trainable. This approach: - Prevents catastrophic forgetting of general language knowledge - Allows heads to adapt to receipt-specific patterns - Reduces training time and memory requirements - Maintains strong baseline performance from pre-trained embeddings

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Dataset Structure
The model is designed for receipt text processing, with example sentences like: - “Thank you, your total is: $32.66” - “500g Organic Canned Tomatoes”
Each training sample contains: 1. Raw sentences: Original text 2. Input IDs: Tokenized input sequences 3. Attention masks: Indicate which tokens are real words vs. padding 4. Classification labels: Sentence-level category (0-3) 5. NER labels: Token-level entity tags (0-4)

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Forward Pass Design

GPU Acceleration
The model and tensors are moved to CUDA when available, enabling parallel computation on GPUs for faster training.


Mini-Batch Processing
Training uses mini-batches to: - Optimize memory usage - Stabilize gradient updates - Enable parallel processing on GPUs


Task-Specific Outputs

Classification: Uses only the CLS token embedding for sentence-level prediction
NER: Uses all token embeddings for sequence-level prediction



Joint Optimization
Both tasks are optimized together: - Losses are computed independently for each head - Total loss is the sum of classification and NER losses - Gradients flow through the shared transformer backbone - This allows shared knowledge to improve both tasks simultaneously


Gradient Clipping
Gradient clipping prevents exploding gradients that could destabilize multi-task learning, especially important when optimizing multiple objectives simultaneously.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Evaluation Metrics
The training loop tracks: - Classification accuracy: Percentage of correctly classified sentences - Classification F1 score: Weighted F1 to handle class imbalance - NER accuracy: Token-level classification accuracy - Separate loss tracking: Monitors each task’s loss independently to detect task imbalance
Both training and validation metrics are computed to ensure the model generalizes well to unseen receipt text.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Training Dynamics
The training process shows how both tasks learn simultaneously, with joint optimization allowing shared knowledge to improve performance on both classification and NER.

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Multi-Task Model Class
The MultiTaskModel class inherits from PyTorch’s nn.Module and implements:

Initialization: Sets up the transformer backbone and both task heads
Forward pass: Routes transformer outputs to classification and NER heads
Flexible architecture: Configurable number of classes and NER labels

title: Multi-Task Sentence Transformer for Receipt Processing
text:
Training Function
The training loop implements: - Epoch-based iteration: Multiple passes through the dataset - Train/validation split: Separate evaluation on held-out data - Loss computation: Combined loss for joint optimization - Metric tracking: Real-time accuracy and F1 score monitoring - Model checkpointing: Ready for saving best models

Living in Edinburgh, the swing between winter darkness and summer’s endless evenings is something you feel deeply. In December, the sun sets before 4pm. By June, it’s still light at 10pm. I wanted to visualize just how dramatic this shift really is.

title: Daylight Hours in Edinburgh
text:
The Visualization



Daylight hours in Edinburgh across 2025


This polar chart shows daylight hours for each day of 2025, arranged in a circle with January at the top, moving clockwise through the year. The distance from the center represents hours of daylight.
The shape tells the story immediately:

Winter solstice (December): Just 7 hours of daylight
Summer solstice (June): Over 17.5 hours of daylight
Difference: A full 10.5 hours — nearly half the day

Edinburgh sits at 55.9°N latitude, which makes for one of the more dramatic seasonal swings you’ll find in a major city. Compare this to somewhere like San Francisco (37.8°N), where the difference is only about 5 hours.

title: Daylight Hours in Edinburgh
text:
The Code
The visualization uses Python with matplotlib for plotting and the astral library to calculate sunrise/sunset times. A Gaussian filter smooths out the DST jumps that would otherwise create ugly discontinuities.


Show the code

"""
Daylight Hours - Polar Visualization
Showing daylight duration across 2025 as a radial chart
"""

# === IMPORTS ===
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.font_manager as fm
import numpy as np
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from astral import LocationInfo
from astral.sun import sun
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d

# === CUSTOM STYLING ===
colors = {
    'daylight': '#f6ad55',      # Warm orange/gold
    'daylight_edge': '#dd6b20', # Darker orange for edge
    'night': '#2d3748',         # Dark blue-gray
    'text': '#4a5568',          # Gray for labels
    'grid': '#e2e8f0',          # Light gray for grid
}

# Adding custom fonts
fm.fontManager.addfont("assets/fonts/Lora-Regular.ttf")
fm.fontManager.addfont("assets/fonts/Lora-SemiBold.ttf")

# Setting matplotlib parameters
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 120,
    "savefig.dpi": 200,
    "font.size": 10,
    "font.family": "Lora",
    "axes.titlesize": 14,
    "axes.titleweight": "semibold",
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
})

# === CONFIGURATION ===
city = LocationInfo("Edinburgh", "UK", "Europe/London", 55.9533, -3.1883)
year = 2025

# === CALCULATE DAYLIGHT DATA ===
daylight_hours = []
day_numbers = []

for day_num in range(365):
    current = datetime(year, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=day_num)
    try:
        s = sun(city.observer, date=current, tzinfo=city.timezone)
        sunrise = s["sunrise"]
        sunset = s["sunset"]
        duration = (sunset - sunrise).total_seconds() / 3600
        daylight_hours.append(duration)
        day_numbers.append(day_num)
    except Exception as e:
        # Use interpolated value if calculation fails
        if daylight_hours:
            daylight_hours.append(daylight_hours[-1])
            day_numbers.append(day_num)

# Convert to numpy arrays
daylight_hours = np.array(daylight_hours)
day_numbers = np.array(day_numbers)

# Smooth the data to remove DST jumps
daylight_smooth = gaussian_filter1d(daylight_hours, sigma=5)

# Convert day of year to angle (radians)
angles = 2 * np.pi * day_numbers / 365

# Close the loop
angles = np.append(angles, angles[0])
daylight_smooth = np.append(daylight_smooth, daylight_smooth[0])

# === PLOTTING ===
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10), subplot_kw={'projection': 'polar'})

# Fill the daylight area
ax.fill(angles, daylight_smooth, color=colors['daylight'], alpha=0.6)
ax.plot(angles, daylight_smooth, color=colors['daylight_edge'], linewidth=2.5)

# Add a center reference circle at minimum daylight
min_hours = daylight_smooth.min()
theta_circle = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
ax.plot(theta_circle, [min_hours] * 100, 
        color=colors['grid'], linewidth=1, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

# Configure the polar plot
ax.set_theta_zero_location('N')   # January at top
ax.set_theta_direction(-1)         # Clockwise

# Set radial limits
ax.set_rlim(0, 20)

# Month labels
month_starts = [0, 31, 59, 90, 120, 151, 181, 212, 243, 273, 304, 334]
month_angles = [2 * np.pi * d / 365 for d in month_starts]
month_names = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 
               'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec']
ax.set_xticks(month_angles)
ax.set_xticklabels(month_names, fontsize=14, color=colors['text'])

# Radial labels
ax.set_rticks([6, 10, 14, 18])
ax.set_yticklabels(['6h', '10h', '14h', '18h'], fontsize=12, color=colors['text'])
ax.set_rlabel_position(45)

# Grid styling
ax.grid(True, color=colors['grid'], linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.7)
ax.spines['polar'].set_color(colors['grid'])

# Title
ax.set_title(f'Daylight Hours in {city.name} in {year}', 
             pad=20, fontsize=24, fontweight='semibold', color=colors['night'])

# Annotations for max/min
max_idx = daylight_smooth[:-1].argmax()
min_idx = daylight_smooth[:-1].argmin()

ax.annotate(f'{daylight_smooth[max_idx]:.1f}h', 
            xy=(angles[max_idx], daylight_smooth[max_idx]),
            xytext=(angles[max_idx], daylight_smooth[max_idx] + 1.5),
            ha='center', fontsize=14, color=colors['text'], fontweight='semibold')

ax.annotate(f'{daylight_smooth[min_idx]:.1f}h', 
            xy=(angles[min_idx], daylight_smooth[min_idx]),
            xytext=(angles[min_idx], daylight_smooth[min_idx] + 1),
            ha='center', fontsize=14, color=colors['text'], fontweight='semibold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('figures/daylight_hours_polar.png', dpi=200, 
            bbox_inches='tight', facecolor='white')
plt.show()
